topic: AI agents (mostly Claude) connected to real cars through a cable

entries.title: 1994 Jeep Cherokee ECU reverse-engineered and rewritten with Claude Code + Codex over a $3 Arduino
entries.outcome: Live ECU reads, drive logging, full program copy, ran its own code, passed California smog test
entries.notable: Claude offered to run the fuel pump and primed the rail for ~10s before being told to stop
entries.critique: A lean tune raises NOx; adding fuel moves toward lambda and reduces NOx while raising CO/HC. Likely masked a mechanical fault rather than fixing it.

patterns: Read-only enforced in code, not in the prompt
Backup before flash, refuse without one
Ground truth beats model quality for CAN reverse engineering
The cable is the moat, not the model
BMW ENET is native on the A90/A91 GR Supra, so BMW tooling works on a Toyota
agent_note: Claude Code dominates this space but does not own it. Codex and Grok appear where several agents were run against each other, and a real Hermes Agent lane exists: the Toyota J2534 MCP server is titled for Hermes, HermesOBD targets Hermes for log analysis, and hermes-automotive-skills is a 102-skill conversion of the Claude Code automotive repo. Most entries are MCP servers, so the agent is swappable.

Frontier model driving a real car

efficiency_findings: Zero hand-written code is now normal: three separate people shipped working in-car systems with none.
The adapter, not the agent, is the failure point. One project lost 3 of 5 days to a dead ELM327 clone; buy a named chip (FTDI/CP2102) or an OBDLink.
Cost per capability is falling: a read-only BMW ECU reader is free software plus a 15 euro cable. The expensive remaining work is firmware signing, not AI.
